Strategy is not the collection of "all good things." Yesterday I watched the conversation between Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi and Mr. Mohammad Fazeli. I hold both of these dear gentlemen in respect, and the points Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi made about macroeconomics were certainly instructive for me and all his students (as they always have been). But at one point in the conversation, Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi said about the 20-year Vision Document: "We drafted this document in 1384, when Ahmadinejad had not yet come, and the document's goals seemed achievable." Linking the failure to realize the Vision Document to the coming of Ahmadinejad (who certainly dealt a great blow to the national interest) does not seem logical to me. The Vision Document was a completely wrong document from the very beginning. It was a beautifully written essay that had no strategic nature (while an upstream document of this kind should naturally have a strategic nature). This document was "the collection of all good and attractive things." Strategy is not of this kind. Strategy means letting go of many good things and setting priorities among other good things, and specifying which good thing we are willing to sacrifice for the sake of another good thing. If these questions are not answered in a document, that document is no longer anything but an essay. I consider it one of my honors that from those very years, when I was teaching strategy, I taught this document as an example of a completely wrong document, and I told my students that this document is not a vision; it is merely pleasing to the eye. That document was wrong on the first day too; with Ahmadinejad or without Ahmadinejad, for Iran or for Saudi Arabia or for America. It was a beautiful essay that appeared poetic and attractive. But my judgment is that anyone who had the slightest literacy in strategy would never have been willing to sign beneath that essay. #Maybe_Temporary

This conversation I had with ChatGPT isn't an ideal…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Large World Models (LWMs)

This conversation I had with ChatGPT isn't an ideal example — it's even a bit misleading.

But it can, to some extent, illustrate the difference between a language model and a world model.

The current wave of AI will presumably die down once the current bubble bursts (and of course its amazing achievements and capabilities will stay with us).

In the next wave, we'll be dealing with large models of the world — LWMs, or Large World Models — that have a better grasp of what's possible and impossible in the physical world.

Of course, even now, the models Tesla uses in the automotive industry and Palantir uses in warfare are of the World Model variety. But even so — whether in terms of the technology and system architecture, or in terms of commercial and widespread access — we're still a very long way from "artificial intelligence capable of understanding the physical world."

This gap — contrary to all the hype — isn't just a matter of scale.

Source: @bamotamem

If Hitler had been killed... On March 13, 1930, just as the car carrying Hitler entered the intersection, a large truck came speeding into the intersection from the right and slammed into the right side of Hitler's car. The exact side where Hitler was sitting in the front seat, next to his driver. The truck pushed the car to the other side of the intersection and came to a stop just before it could run over the car and crush it along with everyone inside. Hitler asked loudly, "Is everyone still alive?" Everyone survived. Though Hitler and two other occupants were left with bruises and contusions. Three years later, he became Chancellor of Germany, and what followed was the carnage of World War II and the Holocaust — a slaughter that claimed tens of millions of lives. If the truck had crushed the car and Hitler had been killed, would those deaths still have happened?

In the Motamem systems thinking discussion about Jared Diamond, one of the members had quoted something from Jared Diamond, and it occurred to me to write a bit there about his latest book, which was published last month. Naturally, there's more room for writing at length on Motamem. But still, I can share a few general points here as well:🖋️ In this book (and in almost all his books from the past thirty years), Diamond is pondering this question: which is greater — the power of "systems and structure" or the power of "people"?I think we Iranians are constantly thinking about this very question. That if so-and-so hadn't been there or hadn't come in such-and-such a year, or if someone else had come instead of someone else, how much would our historical trajectory have changed?🖋️ There are plenty of fascinating points and instructive stories in this book. But methodologically and analytically, I think it's weaker than Diamond's previous works. Still, by a wide margin, Guns, Germs, and Steel remains his best book.🖋️ Diamond believes in the power of influence for both individuals and systems. But he considers the effect of individuals greater in the short term and the effect of systems greater in the long term.🖋️ Diamond is old. One should always view the latest works of thinkers and writers with a forgiving eye. Because their goal is to deliver their remaining notes to us.

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Some people only see and touch the ground they were standing on after they fall.

First explanation

In the early years of Motamem, when we started the daily sentences, sometimes I would also put some of my own words among the daily sentences at the top of the site.

After a while, I felt it wasn't a nice thing to do. The people whose words we were quoting were great people; thinkers, opinion-makers, and at the very least, well-known. Putting my own words among those people's words wasn't a nice thing to do.

I have no problem with saying and writing my words separately (I've been busy with exactly that my whole life). But that thing wasn't mature. In short, consider the photo-note above as the youthful transgressions caused by rawness.

Second explanation

Eleven years ago, when I gave a talk about personal branding, I ended my speech with a sentence that I still like and still stand by. Since the underlying theme of that sentence was also falling, it came to mind now:

Not everyone falls downward,
some fall upward.

Source: @bamotamem

My generation and those older than me, until just a few years ago, when we saw the name Al-Sayyid as a Democratic candidate, we were ready to bet that it was pronounced "El-Sayd." But now we know it's pronounced "Al-Sayyid," and it's even more correct that the "l" isn't pronounced at all (solar lam)!

At one point, Clinton was asked how Republicans in America ended up with someone like Trump (from Nixon to Reagan to the Bushes and then Trump), who is even more extreme compared to his predecessors.

Clinton said: Democratic party became too woke.

Explaining "woke" is beyond the scope of this short piece. But one example (loosely speaking) could be this: if people like the Al-Sayyids and the Mamdanis hadn't multiplied, there wouldn't have been an appetite on the other side for people like Trump either.

I don't want to definitively confirm (or reject) this. But for a moment it crossed my mind.

Footnote: I'm aware that Al-Sayyid and Mamdani came after Trump. I mean people like them who, through a long-term and completely engineered process, gradually found social standing. And of course, the support of some countries in our region, especially Qatar, and the heavy injection of billions of petrodollars into America's intellectual and academic sphere was not without effect in creating an intellectual base of support for them.
